searchText: With TypedTransactions whats the best way to identify thats its typed vs legacy? Per the EIP it states: > TransactionType is a positive unsigned 8-bit number between 0 and 0x7f that represents the type of the transcation Does this mean always taking the first byte and doing something like `txBytes[0] < 0x7f` should result in a telling you if its legacy vs typed? yeah, that's your best bet For our parser I switch off the first byte, if it's a known 2718 type I parse it as such, if it's > 0x7f I assume legacy, otherwise assume it's a new 2718 type I don't know about: https://github.com/INFURA/go-ethlibs/blob/master/eth/transaction_from_raw.go#L54 Is there somewhere in the spec (pre types) that stated the first byte is > 0x7f I’ve been looking but couldn’t find anything <@!322222239850168331> it's just a function of RLP, it's impossible to have a legacy transaction where the first byte < 0x7f since that would be single rlp byte string techincally i don't think it's possible to have a legacy transaction < c0 since they're encoded as lists and 0xc0 is the first list byte The reserved range is actually pretty small IIRC. I think the rationale section of 2718 mentions it. Oh that’s clever Loool Thanks 🙏

excerpts.author: gregthegreek
excerpts.content:
With TypedTransactions whats the best way to identify thats its typed vs legacy? Per the EIP it states:
> TransactionType is a positive unsigned 8-bit number between 0 and 0x7f that represents the type of the transcation
Does this mean always taking the first byte and doing something like `txBytes[0] < 0x7f` should result in a telling you if its legacy vs typed?

excerpts.author: ryanleeschneider
excerpts.content: For our parser I switch off the first byte, if it's a known 2718 type I parse it as such, if it's > 0x7f I assume legacy, otherwise assume it's a new 2718 type I don't know about: https://github.com/INFURA/go-ethlibs/blob/master/eth/transaction_from_raw.go#L54

excerpts.content: techincally i don't think it's possible to have a legacy transaction < c0 since they're encoded as lists and 0xc0 is the first list byte
